text.text: One workspace for the whole studio: clients, the sites you are building, every page on every site, the revision requests that eat hours, and the invoices that keep the lights on. Open the Dashboard on Monday, then work Mine and Overdue. Check Open revisions on a project before you say yes to anything new.
Clients
The businesses the studio builds and cares for sites for.
Projects
Each site build, redesign or care plan, from discovery to launch.
Pages
Every page on every site, from copy to approval.
Revisions
Change requests from clients and testing, with the hours they take.
Invoices
Milestone invoices for each project, tracked here and never paid from here.

This workspace runs a small web studio: clients and their care plans, each site project from discovery to launch, every page and whether its content is in, the change requests that come after sign-off, and the invoices tied to each milestone. Code, designs and files stay in your design tool and repository; this is where the work is planned and tracked.

pages.title: How a project moves through phases

text.text: Every site moves through the same five phases. Each phase ends with something the client signs off, and the next phase starts only after that sign-off. That rhythm keeps projects on schedule and protects you from endless revisions.
The phases

cells.text: Brief, sitemap, content plan, platform choice
Sitemap and brief approved; deposit paid
Home page and one inner page designed, then the rest
Pages built on the platform with real content
Client tests on a staging site; fixes

text.text: Moving a project
Add every page from the sitemap in Discovery, with a due date and an owner.
Move pages through their own statuses: copy drafted, designed, built, approved.
When a phase's sign-off arrives, move the project and send the milestone invoice.
Pages not approved
and
Page progress
show how close the build really is.
Content is the usual delay
Most late launches are waiting on the client's words and photos, not on the studio. Track it honestly:
Content from client
on the project: waiting, partly in or all in.
Copy from client
on each page.
Agree a content deadline at kickoff and put it in the agreement. If it slips, the launch date moves the same number of days.
Choosing the platform

cells.text: Content-heavy sites the client edits often
Simple sites the client wants to run alone

text.text: Example

The Calloway Electric site is in design with services copy drafted and the emergency callouts page not started. Content is only partly in, so the project lead sends the owner three short questions instead of a blank page to fill.
Keep the client close
Send a two-line update every Friday: what moved this week and what you need from them. Silence makes clients nervous, and nervous clients ask for more changes.
A good brief is the cheapest way to avoid three rounds of redesign. Spend an hour with the client before anything is drawn.
The intake call
Ask, and write the answers on the client and project:
What the business does, in one sentence a customer would use
Who the site is for and the one thing they should do on it: call, book, buy or visit
Three sites they like and why, and one they dislike
What exists: logo, brand colors, photos, current site, domain and hosting logins
Who writes the words, and by when
Who approves the work, and how many people need to see it
Budget and launch date, and what drives the date
The brief (one page)

cells.text: The main action and how we will measure it
Who visits and what they need to find
Every page, with one line on its job
Words and examples, not adjectives alone
Who supplies what, and the deadline
Where it is built and who edits it after launch
What this project does not include

text.text: Send the brief for approval before design starts. Sign-off on the brief is the end of discovery.
Pricing and agreement
Fixed fee per project, split into deposit, design milestone and launch balance.
Two rounds of design changes included; more at your hourly rate.
Content deadline written in, with the launch moving if content is late.
Care plan offered from launch, monthly.
Red flags
No one on the client's side can decide.
"We'll write the content later."
A launch date tied to an event less than three weeks away.
Name the risk kindly at intake, and write it in the brief.
Example

Hargrove Tax Advisers' tax season landing page has slipped past its launch date because the copy is still waiting on the client. The brief said the launch moves day for day when content is late, so the new date is agreed without an argument.
Clients will always ask for changes. The goal is not to refuse them but to make each one visible, sorted and, when it is new work, paid for.
What is included
Two rounds of changes on the design.
Fixes to anything that does not match the approved design or does not work.
Small text and image swaps before launch.

text.text: Batching
Work through requests in batches twice a week rather than one at a time. The client gets one update with everything done, and the team is not interrupted all day.
Talking about out-of-scope work
Say yes to the idea and give a price: "Happy to add gift wrap. It is about six hours, so 540 dollars. Shall we do it before launch or right after?" Write the answer on the request.
After launch
Once the site is live, changes belong to the care plan or a new small project. A care plan with a few hours a month turns change requests into steady income.
Example
Tern & Tide asked for a gift wrap option and larger product photos. The photos were in the agreement and are done; gift wrap is new work, logged as out of scope with a six-hour estimate.
A launch should be boring. Every check below is done on the staging site the week before, so launch day is only the switch and a final look.

Launch day

If something breaks

Keep the old site's backup for 30 days. If the new site has a serious problem in the first hours, point the domain back, fix it on staging and launch again. Tell the client straight away, with the plan.
The first week after
Watch for broken links and form errors.
Check analytics daily for odd drops.
